To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The energy gap in amorphous Si is 1.7eV, and the Fermi level is 0.5eV above the valence band edge.
(1) the photoemission from a-Si:H is very similar to the photoemission of a clean Si surface and that (2) the Fermi level of a-Si:H films is pinned at the middle of the bandgap.

the photoelectric yield of amorphous silicon is higher than that of a silicon crystal, the Fermi level is located at the top of the valence band, the density of states is higher than in a crystal, and that the optical transitions are similar to those in a crystal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the properties of amorphous silicon.
the study of amorphous films of semiconductors, particularly silicon.
the study of amorphous silicon and its interface with metals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

amorphous Si is a semiconductor with a bandgap of 1.6 eV and a density of states which is not too different from crystalline Si, but which shows a tail of localized states extending from the Fermi level to about 0.3 eV below the conduction band.
the amorphous silicon is a material of very low electronic quality.

the photoelectric yield from amorphous silicon is not very different from that of the corresponding crystalline silicon and that the photoelectric emission is a sensitive probe of the electronic structure of the disordered material.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
amorphous silicon films are characterized by a large density of states in the gap and a large number of localized states in the valence band.

the photoelectric emission from amorphous silicon is similar to that from a silicon crystal, but that the amorphous films have a higher surface photovoltage than the crystalline material, a lower work function and a smaller density of states.
the amorphous silicon films are semiconducting with an indirect band gap.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the density of states in amorphous silicon (a-Si) is not constant.
the photoelectric yield of amorphous silicon is much higher than that of crystalline silicon.
we have demonstrated the possibility to use photoelectron emission as a probe to determine the density of states of amorphous materials, and to measure the Fermi level position.
